title: Food trust is rebounding but health judgments are moving toward ingredients, processing, labels, and perceived control over the food system
source_unit: International Food Information Council, 2026 IFIC Food & Health Survey: A Focus on Food & Ingredient Safety, September 8, 2026
geography: United States adults ages 18–80, with a first-year Canadian comparison sample

observations.period: 2025–2026; confidence in the U.S. food supply

denominator.unit: U.S. adults ages 18–80 in the IFIC online survey

food_supply_confidence.unit: percent very or somewhat confident in the safety of the U.S. food supply in 2026

year_over_year_change.value: confidence rose from 55% in 2025 to 62% in 2026

historical_boundary.value: 2026 confidence remained below 68% in 2022 and far below the 78% record high in 2012

top_issues.value: pesticides, carcinogens, and foodborne illness remained the most frequently selected top-three food safety concerns

observations.method: Annual IFIC online survey conducted by Greenwald Research through Dynata; fielded March 22–April 8, 2026; weighted by age, education, gender, race/ethnicity, and region to the 2025 Current Population Survey.
observations.uncertainty: This is a weighted consumer-panel survey, not a probability sample or behavioral trace; confidence and concern are perceptions, not direct measures of food contamination, inspection performance, or health outcomes.
observations.subgroup: U.S. consumers, households making food decisions, and people with different demographic and health-related experiences; the public summary emphasizes national trends more than subgroup outcome differences.
observations.counterinterpretation: The confidence rebound may reflect changing salience, reassurance, or survey timing rather than durable institutional trust or safer food conditions.

observations.period: 2022–2026; ingredient simplicity and processing as health criteria

ingredient_simplicity.value: limited or no artificial ingredients or preservatives rose ten percentage points since 2022; limited number of ingredients rose seven points; minimal or no processing rose six points

freshness.value: fresh remained the leading criterion associated with a healthy food, while low in sugar fell out of the top three for the first time

nutrition_shift.value: nutrient-specific criteria such as protein, sugar, sodium, carbohydrate, and saturated fat were less prominent than in the prior year

interpretation.value: health judgments are expanding beyond nutrient content toward ingredients, processing, freshness, naturalness, and environmental production

observations.method: Repeated annual survey question on the top five of 20 criteria used to define a healthy food.
observations.uncertainty: Reported criteria are beliefs and decision cues, not nutrition knowledge, dietary quality, food purchases, or clinical outcomes; wording and changing public discourse may influence trends.
observations.subgroup: U.S. consumers, food shoppers, people managing diet and health, and households navigating labels, prices, and competing health claims.
observations.counterinterpretation: Ingredient simplicity can be a useful heuristic but may also create fear, moralization, or misleading equivalences between processing, safety, nutrition, and health.

observations.period: 2026; food-label regulation, federalism, and public voice

low_awareness.unit: percent reporting hearing little or nothing about state-level food-labeling requirements or ingredient bans

shared_responsibility.unit: percent preferring shared state and federal responsibility for food-ingredient policy

national_rule.unit: percent preferring one national federal rule set

state_only.unit: percent preferring each state to establish its own rules

federal_role.unit: percent favoring some federal role, combining shared and national approaches

observations.method: New IFIC survey questions on awareness of state food regulation and preferred allocation of regulatory responsibility.
observations.uncertainty: Preferences do not establish knowledge of specific rules, implementation performance, or causal support for federal versus state policies; respondents may interpret ‘responsibility’ differently.
observations.subgroup: U.S. consumers, food shoppers, people exposed to state labeling debates, and residents affected by fragmented food rules.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low awareness may reflect limited salience rather than disengagement; support for a federal role may coexist with demands for local adaptation or stronger consumer participation.

core_four_familiarity.unit: percent reporting at least some familiarity with clean, separate, cook, and chill guidance

not_familiar.unit: percent reporting no familiarity with the Core Four guidance

handwashing.unit: percent reporting regularly washing hands in 2026, compared with 83% in 2016 and 97% in 2013

thermometer.unit: percent reporting regular food-thermometer use in 2026, up five points from 2016

label_reach.unit: percent reporting seeing the Safe Handling Instructions label, compared with 67% in 2015

observations.method: Repeated IFIC survey items on food-safety familiarity, self-reported practices, and label exposure.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported practice is subject to recall and social-desirability bias; a trend break after years without measurement may reflect wording, context, or sample differences rather than true behavioral change.
observations.subgroup: U.S. household food preparers, consumers using labels and guidance, and people with different cooking routines and access to food-safety information.
observations.counterinterpretation: Label information may reach fewer people while remaining highly useful to those who see it; declines in some practices do not establish increased foodborne illness.

related_sources.claim: Earlier IFIC Food & Health survey materials provide prior-year food, health, affordability, and trust context.
National Restaurant Association consumer tracking provides complementary evidence on food spending, affordability, and household adaptation.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. food-culture and public-trust route from food-supply confidence and ingredient concerns through health heuristics, labeling awareness, federalism preferences, household preparation, and everyday risk management. It is a weighted online consumer-panel survey commissioned by IFIC, not a probability sample, behavioral trace, clinical study, or causal measure of food safety or dietary health.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official IFIC September 8, 2026 publication page and 39-page PDF were reviewed for sample and weighting, food-supply confidence, top food-safety issues, ingredient and processing criteria, state-regulation awareness, federal/state preferences, food-safety guidance familiarity, self-reported practices, and label exposure.
